'''Cuomo:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Mario Cuomo]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[George Pataki]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNY}} The '''1994 New York gubernatorial election''' was an [[election]] for the state [[Governor of New York|governorship]] held on November 8, 1994. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Mario Cuomo]] ran for a fourth term, but was defeated by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[George Pataki]] in an [[Upset (competition)|upset]] victory. Pataki had previously been described by the ''[[New York Daily News]]'' as "a little-known Republican state senator."{{cite news |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]] |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/news/politics/mario-cuomo-new-york-governor-dead-82-article-1.2063258 |title=Mario Cuomo, former New York governor, dead at 82 |author1=Kenneth Lovett |author2=Larry McShane |date=January 5, 2015}} The conservative ''[[New York Post]]'' attributed the result to how voters "had grown tired of the 12-year incumbent Cuomo and his liberalism."{{cite news |newspaper=[[The New York Post]] |url=https://nypost.com/2015/01/01/former-new-york-governor-mario-cuomo-dead-at-82 |title=Former New York Gov. Mario Cuomo dead at 82 |author1=Carl Campanile |author2=Larry Celona |author3=Leonard Greene |date=January 1, 2015}} Pataki's victory was one of the most notable of the 1994 "[[Republican Revolution]]" midterm elections, which also ousted governors in Alabama, New Mexico, and Texas. This is the last time a governor of New York lost re-election. This would be the last gubernatorial race until [[2022 New York gubernatorial election|2022]] that was decided by a single-digit margin. This is the only election (primary or general) where a member of the Cuomo family lost [[Staten Island]]. ==Democratic primary== === Candidates === * [[Mario Cuomo]], incumbent governor * [[Lenora Fulani]], activist and [[perennial candidate]]{{cite news |newspaper=[[The New York Daily News]] |url=https://www.nydailynews.com/opinion/masters-deception-article-1.1216664 |title=Revealed: How cult-like band exploits voter deception to wield political power in N.Y.C. |date=December 10, 2012}} ==== Withdrew ==== * [[Roy Innis]], national chair of the [[Congress of Racial Equality]] and [[1993 New York City mayoral election#Democratic primary|1993 candidate]] for New York City mayor ===Campaign=== Cuomo faced two primary challengers: [[Lenora Fulani]], a perennial [[New Alliance Party]] candidate, and [[Roy Innis]], national chair of the [[Congress of Racial Equality]] and a failed challenger to New York City mayor David Dinkins in the 1993 election. Innis ultimately failed to submit petition signatures.{{cite news |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/15/nyregion/moynihan-won-t-fight-the-petitions-of-sharpton.html |title=Moynihan Won't Fight The Petitions Of Sharpton |date=July 15, 1994}}{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/11/nyregion/tilting-at-the-same-windmill-but-on-a-faster-steed.html |title=Tilting at the Same Windmill, but on a Faster Steed |date=11 September 1994 |work=The New York Times}} Fulani's bid was generally considered a Quixotic, losing effort. Cuomo refused to debate her, and Fulani made it plain that she sought to draw [[African Americans]] away from the Democratic Party. [[Adam Clayton Powell IV]] was the only elected official to endorse her candidacy, and Fulani was also far outstripped in fundraising. ===Results=== On September 13, 1994, Cuomo handily defeated Fulani.{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/14/nyregion/the-1994-campaign-the-overview-pataki-easily-wins-the-right-to-oppose-cuomo.html |title=Pataki Easily Wins the Right to Oppose Cuomo |date=14 September 1994 |work=The New York Times}}[[File:1994 New York Democratic gubernatorial primary election results map by county (vote share).svg|thumb|300px|Results by county {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#678cd7|Cuomo}} |{{legend|#8da9e2|50–60%}} |{{legend|#678cd7|60–70%}} |{{legend|#4170cd|70–80%}} |{{legend|#3358a2|80–90%}} }}|center]] {{Election box begin no change | title = 1994 Democratic gubernatorial primary{{citation needed|date=October 2026}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Mario Cuomo]] (incumbent) | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 548,762 | percentage = 79.45 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Lenora Fulani]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 141,918 | percentage = 20.55 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 690,680 | percentage= 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== === Candidates === * [[Evan G. Galbraith]], former [[List of ambassadors of the United States to France|U.S. ambassador to France]] * [[Herbert London]], founder of the [[Gallatin School of Individualized Study|Gallatin Divison]] of [[New York University]] and 1990 Conservative Party nominee for governor (''also running as Conservative'') * [[George Pataki]], [[New York State Senate|state senator]] from [[Peekskill, New York|Peekskill]] (''also running as Conservative'') * [[Richard M. Rosenbaum]], former chair of the [[New York Republican State Committee]]{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/23/nyregion/gop-leader-will-run-for-governor-as-moderate.html|title=G.O.P. Leader Will Run For Governor as 'Moderate'|date=23 March 1994|work=The New York Times}} (''also running as Independence Party candidate'') ==== Withdrew ==== * [[Bill Green (New York politician)|Bill Green]], former [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] ''(endorsed Rosenbaum)''{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/19/nyregion/ex-rep-green-announces-for-governor.html|title=Ex-Rep. Green Announces for Governor|date=19 March 1994|work=The New York Times}} ==== Declined ==== * J. Patrick Barrett, businessman and former chair of the [[New York Republican State Committee]]{{cite web|last=Sack |first=Kevin |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/21/nyregion/gop-race-for-governor-is-narrowed.html |title=G.O.P. Race For Governor Is Narrowed |location=New York |work=The New York Times |date=1994-05-21 |access-date=2016-08-08}} * [[Al D'Amato]], [[United States Senate|U.S. senator]] since 1981{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/10/20/us/d-amato-skips-a-race.html|title=D'Amato Skips a Race|date=20 October 1993|work=The New York Times}} Initially, U.S. senator [[Al D'Amato]] was expected to run as the Republican and Conservative nominee. He began to publicly criticize Cuomo in September 1993 when he claimed that New York had become "the taxasaurus and spendasaurus capital of the nation" during Cuomo's tenure.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/09/28/nyregion/d-amato-raising-funds-assails-cuomo-s-record-as-governor.html|title=D'Amato, Raising Funds, Assails Cuomo's Record as Governor|date=28 September 1993|work=The New York Times}} However, D'Amato decided not to run within the month, predicting (accurately) that his party could take control of the Senate in the 1994 elections, which would elevate him to chairman of the [[United States Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs|Senate Banking Committee]]. [[Lewis Lehrman]], the [[1982 New York gubernatorial election|1982]] gubernatorial nominee who narrowly lost to Cuomo, also publicly flirted with a run, but ultimately didn't mount a candidacy.{{Cite web|last=Staff|title=LEHRMAN WEIGHS MAKING ANOTHER RUN FOR GOVERNOR|url=https://buffalonews.com/news/lehrman-weighs-making-another-run-for-governor/article_3073b9a1-8270-5373-97ba-2d01ae2f5eb3.html|access-date=2021-10-11|website=The Buffalo News|date=29 July 1991 |language=en}} After considering other potential candidates, D'Amato and Republican chairman [[William Powers (politician)|William Powers]] endorsed state senator [[George Pataki]], a candidate who had potential to win support from the party's moderate and conservative factions.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/11/10/nyregion/peekskill-legislator-to-seek-governor-nomination.html|title=Peekskill Legislator to Seek Governor Nomination|date=10 November 1993|work=The New York Times}} [[Herbert London]], who had run against the Republicans as the Conservative nominee in the prior election, declared his candidacy on October 5, 1993. He ran on a platform of [[tax cut]]s, reductions to state Medicaid and welfare payments, and [[social conservatism]], criticizing both Cuomo and D'Amato. However, London's social conservatism and poor fundraising caused many party leaders to believe that he had no chance of defeating Cuomo.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/10/05/nyregion/conservative-is-joining-gop-race-for-governor.html|title=Conservative Is Joining G.O.P. Race for Governor|date=5 October 1993|work=The New York Times}}{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/01/31/nyregion/candidate-seeks-new-armor-for-crusade-against-cuomo.html|title=Candidate Seeks New Armor For Crusade Against Cuomo|date=31 January 1994|work=The New York Times}} On January 4, 1994, Manhattan businessman and former ambassador [[Evan G. Galbraith|Evan Galbraith]] launched an [[Exploratory committee|exploratory bid]]. Galbraith had also previously been a candidate for governor in 1990, but a court had declared him eligible due to residency issues.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/01/05/nyregion/new-gubernatorial-entry-gets-financial-backing.html|title=New Gubernatorial Entry Gets Financial Backing|date=5 January 1994|work=The New York Times}}{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/04/29/nyregion/galbraith-a-former-envoy-enters-the-gubernatorial-race.html|title=Galbraith, a Former Envoy, Enters the Gubernatorial Race|date=29 April 1994|work=The New York Times}} The field was rounded out in March 1994, when Pataki entered the race officially with support from D'Amato and Powers. He was quickly followed by former U.S. representative [[Bill Green (New York politician)|Bill Green]], who positioned himself as a moderate alternative to Pataki and London, and former party chair [[Richard Rosenbaum]], who ran on a liberal [[Rockefeller Republican]] platform, calling for Medicaid financing of abortion and tighter restrictions on firearms. Former party chairman J. Patrick Barrett, a businessman from Syracuse, who was expected to join the race, declined on May 20 when he came to the conclusion that he could not obtain the necessary support at the state convention. ===Campaign=== ==== Preconvention campaign ==== Pataki was opposed by Senate majority leader [[Ralph J. Marino|Ralph Marino]] over Pataki's association with the influential conservative, anti-tax [[advocacy group]] Change New York, which had worked to prevent Marino's reelection. Organizations on both sides of the abortion debate also criticized Pataki's moderate approach to the issue.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/15/nyregion/state-senator-pataki-formally-declares-challenge-to-cuomo.html|title=State Senator Pataki Formally Declares Challenge to Cuomo|date=15 March 1994|work=The New York Times}} Galbraith formally declared his candidacy on April 29; by this time, however, most conservatives had coalesced around either London or Pataki. Galbraith received endorsements from several notable figures including [[Henry Kissinger]] and [[William F. Buckley Jr.]] Galbraith supporters argued that he held similar positions to London but appealed to a larger base of voters. Among the liberals, Richard Rosenbaum amassed a large campaign [[war chest]] of about $1.2 million. He decided against trying to secure an automatic ballot spot through the convention process because he did not believe he could attain the required 25 percent of the delegate vote. Instead, Rosenbaum opted to petition his way onto the ballot.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/23/nyregion/gop-leader-will-run-for-governor-as-moderate.html|title=G.O.P. Leader Will Run For Governor as 'Moderate'|date=23 March 1994|work=The New York Times}}{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/26/nyregion/republicans-and-conservatives-solidify-efforts-against-cuomo.html|title=Republicans and Conservatives Solidify Efforts Against Cuomo|date=26 May 1994|work=The New York Times}}{{cite web|last=Sack |first=Kevin |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/20/nyregion/political-notes-seeking-a-nomination-without-a-party-s-help.html |title=POLITICAL NOTES - Seeking a Nomination Without a Party's Help |location=New York |work=The New York Times |date=1994-03-20 |access-date=2016-08-08}} Bill Green did enter the convention process, claiming to be conservative on fiscal issues and "sensibly compassionate" on social issues. His bid was badly damaged when Conservative Party chair Michael Long indicated that Conservatives were unlikely to support him if nominated, implicitly threatening a repeat of the 1990 election, in which the Conservatives had split the vote against Cuomo and nearly surpassed Republicans as the state's second party.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/19/nyregion/ex-rep-green-announces-for-governor.html|title=Ex-Rep. Green Announces for Governor|date=19 March 1994|work=The New York Times}} ==== Convention results ==== At the Republican convention, Pataki won the overwhelming support of the delegates present. Herbert London, the runner-up, fell short of the 25% showing that he needed to obtain a place on the party's primary ballot.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/24/nyregion/gop-backs-a-legislator-to-oppose-cuomo.html|title=G.O.P. London was nominated for the position of [[New York State Comptroller|state comptroller]], consolidating his support behind Pataki.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/05/26/nyregion/republicans-and-conservatives-solidify-efforts-against-cuomo.html|title=Republicans and Conservatives Solidify Efforts Against Cuomo|date=26 May 1994|work=The New York Times}} On May 31, Green withdrew from the race and endorsed Rosenbaum.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/06/01/nyregion/green-dropping-out-of-governor-race-backing-rosenbaum.html|title=Green Dropping Out Of Governor Race; Backing Rosenbaum|date=1 June 1994|agency=Associated Press|work=The New York Times}} ====Results==== Pataki defeated Rosenbaum in the Republican primary easily. Rosenbaum]], former chair of the New York Republican State Committee (''also running as Republican''){{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/15/nyregion/1994-campaign-governor-s-race-swiping-cuomo-pataki-gives-plan-governing.html|title=SWIPING AT CUOMO, PATAKI GIVES OUT PLAN ON GOVERNING|date=15 September 1994|work=The New York Times}} === Aftermath === After Rosenbaum withdrew as the nominee, businessman [[Tom Golisano]] was nominated and added to the general election ballot on September 28.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/29/nyregion/campaign-trail-cuomo-the-ballplayer-helps-cuomo-the-candidate.html|title=Campaign Trail; Cuomo the Ballplayer Helps Cuomo the Candidate|date=29 September 1994|work=The New York Times}} ==Libertarian nomination== === Candidates === * Joseph Brennan * Dottie Lou Brokaw, nominee for lieutenant governor in 1990 * James Ostrowski, [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]] attorney{{Cite news |last=Sack |first=Kevin |date=1994-04-24 |title=With Eyes Open Wide, Libertarians Choose Stern |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/04/24/nyregion/with-eyes-open-wide-libertarians-choose-stern.html |access-date=2026-10-01 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} * Norma Segal * [[Howard Stern]], radio [[shock jock]] and host of ''[[The Howard Stern Show]]'' === Campaign === New York City radio personality [[Howard Stern]] announced his candidacy for governor on his [[The Howard Stern Show|nationally syndicated radio show]] on March 22, 1994. Stern ran on a platform of reinstating [[capital punishment]], letting road crews work only at night, staggering highway tolls to prevent traffic jams, and resigning from office as soon as these goals were accomplished.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/04/03/us/gov-howard-stern-some-fail-to-see-humor.html|title=Gov. Howard Stern? Some Fail to See Humor|date=3 April 1994|work=The New York Times}} === Results === Stern won the party's nomination by a two-thirds majority on the first ballot at their state convention on April 23, 1994. {{Election box begin no change | title = 1994 Libertarian state convention ballot{{citation needed|date=October 2026}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Howard Stern]] | party = Libertarian Party (United States) | votes = 287 | percentage = 75.33 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = James Ostrowski | party = Libertarian Party (United States) | votes = 34 | percentage = 8.92 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Norma Segal | party = Libertarian Party (United States) | votes = 24 | percentage = 6.30 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Dottie Lou Brokaw | party = Libertarian Party (United States) | votes = 22 | percentage = 5.77 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Joseph Brennan | party = Libertarian Party (United States) | votes = 10 | percentage = 2.63 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Scattering | party = Independent (politics) | votes = 4 | percentage = 1.05 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 381 | percentage= 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} === Aftermath === Stern refused to file the financial disclosures required by law of any party seeking to hold public office. He filed suit against the state of New York, arguing that the applicable law violated his right to privacy and freedom of association. When the court denied his petition for an injunction, Stern called a press conference on August 4, 1994, and withdrew from the race.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/05/nyregion/for-stern-it-s-balk-radio-he-ends-bid-for-governor.html|title=For Stern, It's Balk Radio: He Ends Bid for Governor|date=5 August 1994|work=The New York Times}} He was replaced by activist [[Robert L. Schulz]].{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} ==General election== === Candidates === * [[Mario Cuomo]], incumbent governor since 1983 (Democratic, Liberal) ** Running mate: Stan Lundine, incumbnet lieutenant governor since 1987 * [[Tom Golisano]], CEO and founder of [[Paychex]] (Independence) * Lawrence Lane (Socialist Workers) * [[George Pataki]], state senator from [[Peekskill, New York|Peekskill]] (Republican, Conservative, Tax Cut Now) ** Running mate: [[Betsy McCaughey]], [[Manhattan Institute for Policy Research|Manhattan Institute]] editorialist and leading critic of the [[Clinton health care plan of 1993|Clinton health care plan]] * [[Robert L. Schulz]], [[Queensbury, New York|Queensbury]] political activist and [[tax protester]] (Libertarian) ** Running mate: Stan Dworkin, former [[Rockland County, New York|Rockland County]] legislator * Robert T. Walsh (Right to Life) ==== Withdrew ==== * [[Richard M. Rosenbaum]], former chair of the New York Republican State Committee (Independence) ''(withdrew September 14; endorsed Pataki'') * [[Howard Stern]], radio [[shock jock]] and host of ''[[The Howard Stern Show]]'' (Libertarian) ''(withdrew August 4)'' === Campaign === Though early in the campaign, Cuomo led by as much as ten points, Pataki was eventually able to tie him due to his difficulty in defending his record. Pataki pledged to cut income taxes by 25 percent which appealed to voters in an economic downturn.{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} One key issue in the election was [[capital punishment]]. Cuomo was a staunch opponent, while Pataki supported it, and opinion polling showed that most New Yorkers agreed due to high crime rates over the prior two decades. Republican ads highlighted the case of [[Arthur Shawcross]], a serial killer convicted of manslaughter who was paroled by New York in 1987 and committed additional murders while on release.
